title: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase When It Means Sex?
paragraphs: “HE WENT IN TO HER”: Why Does the Bible Use This Phrase When It Means Sex?
The strange biblical expression we usually read past may reveal something far deeper about sex, intimacy, sin, covenant—and the God who refuses to leave broken people where He found them.
There are phrases in the Bible that your eyes learn to glide over.
You read them.
You think you understand them.
And then one day you stop.
Wait.
What did that just say?
“He went in to her.”

If you grew up reading older English translations of Scripture, you have probably encountered language like this without giving it much thought. Abraham “went in unto Hagar.” Judah was told to “go in unto” his brother’s wife. Samson “went in unto” a woman in Gaza.
We know what happened.
The context makes it unmistakable.
They had sexual relations.
So why doesn’t the Bible simply say that?
Why this strange language of entering, going in, knowing, lying with, becoming one flesh?
Is Scripture trying to sanitize sex?
Is it embarrassed by the human body?
Were the translators too uncomfortable to say what the Hebrew actually said?
Or have we been reading an ancient world through modern ears and therefore missing something that would have been far more natural to the Bible’s first hearers?
Because the answer takes us somewhere much deeper than an old-fashioned euphemism.
It takes us into the Hebrew language.
Into marriage.
Into human vulnerability.
Into sexual sin.
Into covenant.
Into shame.
Into the bedroom.
Into Eden.
And eventually...
to Jesus Christ.
Consider Genesis 16.
Sarai cannot conceive. Years have passed. God's promise seems painfully slow. So she gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram.
Then Genesis 16:4 says:
וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר וַתַּהַר
Vayyāvoʾ ʾel-Hāgār vattahar.
Very literally:
“And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived.”
There it is.
The Hebrew verb at the center of the expression is בּוֹא — bôʾ.
Its basic meaning is remarkably ordinary.
To come.
To go.
To enter.
The word itself does not automatically mean “have sex.”
That matters.

Biblical Hebrew frequently allows context to carry meaning that modern English expects the verb itself to spell out. When bôʾ is used in certain relational settings—someone “going in to” a woman—the surrounding narrative can make sexual intercourse unmistakable.
So when an older English Bible says that a man “went in unto her,” it is often preserving the shape of the Hebrew expression more closely than contemporary English normally would.
Modern translations frequently make the intended meaning more explicit because “went in to her” no longer naturally communicates sexual intercourse to many English readers.
But Scripture has another expression that may be even more fascinating.
Genesis 4:1 says:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ
Vehaʾadam yādaʿ ʾet-Ḥavvah ʾishtô.
The key word is:
יָדַע — yādaʿ
“To know.”
Adam “knew” Eve his wife, and she conceived Cain.
Again, the context tells us this is sexual union.
But notice something beautiful.
The Bible does not have only one mechanical vocabulary for sex.
Sometimes Scripture speaks of “lying with” someone.
Sometimes of “going in to” someone.
Genesis describes husband and wife as becoming “one flesh.”
And sometimes the Bible uses the astonishing language of “knowing.”
That does not mean every occurrence of yādaʿ is sexual. Far from it. It is an extremely common Hebrew verb for knowing.
Context determines its meaning.
But when Scripture uses it for marital intercourse, the expression is striking.
Because biblical sexuality was never meant to be reduced to two bodies consuming one another.
God created sex before pornography existed.
Before adultery.
Before prostitution.
Before lust became an industry.
Before bodies became products.
Before people learned to swipe through human beings as though they were merchandise.
Before anyone learned to separate physical nakedness from personal covenant.
Go all the way back.
Before the scandal came the garden.
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25).
Read that slowly.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
No hiding.
No comparison.
No secret browser history.
No memories of betrayal.
No fear of abandonment.
No performance.
No exploitation.
No wondering whether you are attractive enough.
No wondering whether this person will disappear tomorrow.
No shame.
Then sin entered.
And what is one of the first things humanity did?
They covered themselves.
They hid.
That is not accidental.
Sin did not merely damage humanity's relationship with God.
It fractured the human experience of being seen.
Suddenly nakedness could feel dangerous.
Exposure could produce shame.
Desire could become distorted.
What God created as good could now be exploited, weaponized, commercialized, idolized and separated from covenant faithfulness.
And maybe that is where this stops being an interesting Hebrew lesson and starts getting uncomfortably personal.
Because perhaps you clicked this article because the phrase sounded strange.
Maybe even a little provocative.
But perhaps underneath the curiosity is a story nobody knows.
Maybe sex has never felt simple to you.
Maybe somebody introduced you to pornography before you were old enough to understand what it was doing to your imagination.
Maybe you keep deleting the history and returning to the same websites.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are doing fine.
You worship.
You quote Scripture.
You post Christian content.
You say “God bless you.”
But there is another version of you that appears when nobody is watching.
Maybe you crossed a boundary you promised God you would never cross.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel loved.
Maybe you gave your body hoping someone would give you their heart.
They didn't.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe someone cheated on you.
Maybe your marriage has been carrying sexual wounds for years, but neither of you knows how to talk about them anymore.
Maybe what should have represented tenderness now reminds you of rejection.
Maybe someone used your trust against you.
Maybe something sexual happened to you that you did not choose.
If so, another person's sin against you is not something Scripture asks you to pretend was acceptable. The Gospel does not require calling evil good in order to offer healing.
And maybe your story is different.
Maybe you were the one who sinned.
That sentence is harder.
Because Christianity is not merely about identifying what somebody else did to us.
Eventually the Gospel brings us before God without costumes.
No excuses.
No carefully cropped version of ourselves.
Just truth.
And this is where Scripture becomes terrifyingly beautiful.
God already knows.
The God who asked Adam, “Where are you?” was not suffering from a lack of information.
Adam was hiding.
God was calling him out.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide behind religion.
We hide behind humor.
We hide behind relationships.
We hide behind private browsing.
We hide behind “everybody does it.”
We hide behind trauma when trauma explains some of our wounds but cannot make every choice righteous.
We hide behind shame.
We even hide behind ministry.
But eventually Christ walks directly toward the place we desperately hoped He would avoid.
Not because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
Because He intends to save them.
Look at Jesus.

A woman caught in adultery is dragged publicly into His presence in John 8. Whatever questions surround the textual history of that passage, the scene preserved in the Christian tradition powerfully depicts something thoroughly consistent with Christ's call to both mercy and holiness.
Her accusers want condemnation.
Jesus refuses their hypocrisy.
But He does not rename sin.
Grace does not become moral indifference.
His mercy moves toward transformation.
Neither condemnation from self-righteous people nor permission to remain unchanged.
Grace.
Then holiness.
That pattern matters.
Because somewhere along the way, many people began believing that repentance means God standing over a filthy sinner saying, “Look what you did.”
The Gospel gives us something far more astonishing.
The holy Son of God takes sinners seriously enough to tell us the truth...
and loves sinners deeply enough to bear judgment Himself.
At the cross, Jesus was not pretending sin did not matter.
The cross is precisely how seriously sin matters.
Christ “suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
That includes sexual sin.
Adultery.
Fornication.
Pornography.
Lust.
Secret fantasy.
Deception.
Sexual selfishness.
Things you did.
Things you regret.
Things you wish you could erase.
But hear this carefully:
You cannot erase your past.
Jesus can redeem a sinner.
There is a difference.
Christianity does not teach that salvation gives us a time machine.
Consequences can remain.
Memories can remain.
People we hurt may still need time.
Trust may have to be rebuilt.
Repentance may require painful honesty and concrete change.
Grace does not make consequences imaginary.
Grace means consequences do not have to become your final identity before God.
Paul wrote to Christians in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sexual and other sin:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes the Gospel-shaped reversal:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Some of you need that word more than another motivational speech.
Were.
Your sin may explain part of your history.
It does not have to dictate your eternity.
Your worst night does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your hidden browser history is not more powerful than the Gospel.
Your adultery is not stronger than Christ.
Your sexual past is not stronger than Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than Christ.
But grace is not permission to keep returning lovingly to the chains from which Christ calls you.
Jesus does not merely offer relief from guilt.
He calls us to Himself.
Repentance means turning.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes after falling again.
But turning.
Coming into the light.
Jesus said, “The truth shall make you free” (John 8:32).
And perhaps the truth you need tonight is this:
You have spent years trying to become clean enough to approach the One who alone can cleanse you.
Stop hiding.
Come to Christ.
Not after you fix yourself.
Now.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him your disordered desires.
Bring Him the relationship you know dishonors Him.
Bring Him the secret account.
Bring Him the messages you would panic if your spouse discovered.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath the lust.
Bring Him the anger underneath the promiscuity.
Bring Him the ache underneath the pornography.
Bring Him the entire ruined story.
And repent.
Not because repentance purchases His love.
Because Jesus Christ is worthy of your whole life.
The Savior who died for sinners did not remain dead.
He rose.
And the risen Christ still makes dead things live.
That is why the Bible's sexual language matters.
“He went in to her” is not some embarrassing relic Christians need to apologize for.

It reminds us that Scripture comes to us through real human languages, cultures and literary conventions. We should resist forcing twenty-first-century English assumptions onto ancient Hebrew expressions.
The Hebrew בּוֹא — bôʾ does not secretly mean “sex” every time it appears.
Context matters.
יָדַע — yādaʿ does not secretly mean “sex” every time either.
Context matters.
Good biblical interpretation does not build theology from an English euphemism while ignoring Hebrew usage.
But once we understand the language, something larger emerges.
The Bible is extraordinarily realistic about human sexuality.
It contains marital intimacy and sexual sin.
Faithfulness and adultery.
Conception and infertility.
Desire and exploitation.
Purity and prostitution.
Broken families and restored people.
It does not give us airbrushed saints.
Abraham's household becomes painfully complicated after Hagar.
Judah's story contains sexual scandal.
David's house carries devastating consequences from sexual sin and abuse of power.
Samson's appetites repeatedly place him in danger.
Yet Scripture's central story is not humanity climbing toward moral perfection.
It is God moving toward sinners in redeeming grace.
And ultimately He comes in Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
You thought this article would explain a strange phrase about sex.
Perhaps God used that curiosity to bring you somewhere else entirely.
To the locked room inside yourself.
To the thing you keep refusing to name.
To the realization that being sexually desired is not the same thing as being loved.
Being touched is not the same thing as being known.
Being wanted for one night is not the same thing as covenant.
Pornography can show you thousands of naked bodies while teaching you almost nothing about genuine intimacy.
Lust says:
What can I take from you?
Love asks:
How can I faithfully seek your good?
And the Gospel goes further.
Jesus says:
I give Myself for you.
That is why Christian sexual ethics cannot finally be understood as God arbitrarily trying to keep people from pleasure.
Our bodies belong to the Lord.
Paul's answer to sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6 is rooted in identity, redemption and union with Christ.
“You are not your own.”
“You are bought with a price.”
Therefore:
“Glorify God in your body.”
Your body matters because Christ matters.
Your sexuality matters because discipleship includes the body.
Your private life matters because Jesus is Lord when the church service ends.
And if this is exposing something hidden, don't turn conviction into another five minutes of religious emotion.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Get accountable.
If another person is involved, stop using spiritual language to justify what Scripture calls sin.
If pornography owns your nights, bring the battle into the light with mature, trustworthy Christian accountability and practical barriers.
If you have wounded your spouse, repentance means more than feeling terrible. Seek forgiveness, accept appropriate consequences, and begin rebuilding truthfully.

And if sexual abuse was committed against you, do not confuse somebody else's crime with your guilt. Seek safe, trustworthy pastoral and professional support. Christ's compassion toward the wounded is not diminished by what another person did.
This is where Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create another corner of the internet where Christians pretend.
But to keep pointing exhausted, wounded, tempted, ashamed and hungry people toward Scripture and toward Jesus Christ.
Use them.
Share them.
Put truth into your mind before the world fills it with something else.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns forgiveness.
It cannot.
It should not be presented that way.
Scripture specifically teaches that Christian giving must not be extracted through pressure: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That share costs nothing.
Someone may read the title because they are curious about sex...
and encounter Jesus before they reach the end.
And comment.
Not for appearances.
Not because you need to tell strangers every detail of your past.
But because sometimes one honest sentence is the moment hiding begins to lose its power.
Someone scrolling beneath you may discover they are not the only Christian fighting.
Someone may finally confess.
Someone may finally pray.
Someone may finally return.
Someone may finally discover that Christianity was never the story of spotless people congratulating themselves for being better than everybody else.
It is the story of a spotless Savior rescuing sinners.
So now we return to that strange sentence.
“He went in to her.”
At first it sounded like an awkward old expression for sex.
But behind it was a doorway into something much larger.
The Bible knows exactly how complicated human desire can become.
It knows what people do with their bodies.
It knows what people do in darkness.
It knows how families fracture.
It knows how shame makes us hide.
It knows scandal.
And still...
page after page...
God keeps moving toward fallen humanity until, in the fullness of time, the Word becomes flesh.
Jesus enters our ruined story.
Not to participate in our sin.
To carry sinners out of it.
He touches lepers.
He eats with sinners.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes the repentant.
He goes to a cross.
He sheds His blood.
He rises from the grave.
And He still calls people out of darkness.
Maybe tonight...
He is calling you.
The deepest question is no longer why the Bible says, “he went in to her.”
The question is whether you will keep hiding when Christ is calling you into the light.
Because the scandal may explain how your story broke...
but grace gets the final word when the Author is Jesus.
